content:
I give talks about Lean to mathematicians and I often get the question "how do you know Lean has got no bugs". I have two stock answers to this; the short one is "I trust Lean more than I trust you" and the longer one is "there's this tool called comparator and there are multiple kernels, so the situation is analogous to using a possibly-buggy computer algebra system to factor a large number into two smaller ones; at the end of the day it's easy to just multiply the two smaller ones together and check you get the larger one, and then who cares if the system is buggy, the theorem is true anyway".

But yesterday I had someone who knew what they were talking about and who asked a more detailed question (fortunately after the talk was over rather than during it) and I realised that actually I didn't understand things well enough to give a coherent answer.

The question was this. Say a proof is AI-generated and the AI does the following malicious thing: finds a bug in GMP with e.g. some huge integers causing an overflow problem, proves false using it, and then deduces the Riemann hypothesis. At what, if any, point during the comparator and/or check-with-alternative-kernel procedure does this approach become unstuck?
Turn off gmp?

As far as i know, other kernels don't have to use GMP. So an exploit on GMP is unlikely to be exploitable across different kernels.
Also, a an exploit on GMP in one kernel is unlikely to give rise to the same exploit on another kernel even if this one uses GMP.

Matthew Ballard said:

Turn off gmp?

That's not really possible as a user.

The question was this. Say a proof is AI-generated and the AI does the following malicious thing: finds a bug in GMP with e.g. some huge integers causing an overflow problem, proves false using it, and then deduces the Riemann hypothesis. At what, if any, point during the comparator and/or check-with-alternative-kernel procedure does this approach become unstuck?

If you want to prevent this type of scenario you have to use comparator with enable_nanoda set to true (and an installed nanoda of course). Nanoda uses num-bigint which is a pure Rust implementation of bignum arithmetic. While the code might be inspired by GMP (I don't know if it is) this is a fully separate implementation in another (notably memory safe) programming language so it should be unlikely that they allow for the exact same bugs.
This still presents a conundrum from the user facing side. If a proof presented by a third party passes in one kernel and fails in another, which kernel is the buggy one?
That doesnt really matter much, you know that the proof is not accepted and thats all you need. Which kernel is the buggy one can be determined by the respective kernel authors

I thought it was as simple as “use windows” at some point. ;)
I don't know the windows config from the top of my head but even if that is true you would be stopped by the fact that comparator can only operate on Linux.

At what, if any, point during the comparator and/or check-with-alternative-kernel procedure does this approach become unstuck?

If you want to prevent this type of scenario you have to use comparator with enable_nanoda set to true (and an installed nanoda of course). Nanoda uses num-bigint which is a pure Rust implementation of bignum arithmetic. While the code might be inspired by GMP (I don't know if it is) this is a fully separate implementation in another (notably memory safe) programming language so it should be unlikely that they allow for the exact same bugs.

fwiw it has been mentioned in passing on the num-bigint repo that "just reimplement the GMP version of X" is discouraged to avoid GPL compatibility issues (num-bigint is Apache-2.0/MIT).

I've never directly worked on bignum code so I don't know how difficult or time consuming it would actually be, but having built-in bignums instead of using an external dependency would be neat.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Say a proof is AI-generated and the AI does the following malicious thing: finds a bug in GMP with e.g. some huge integers causing an overflow problem, proves false using it, and then deduces the Riemann hypothesis. At what, if any, point during the comparator and/or check-with-alternative-kernel procedure does this approach become unstuck?

Adding to the answers above: until we reach the shining city on a hill of having a top to bottom verified hardware and software stack and verified libraries for all implementing code, what we can do with existing solutions is raise percentages/add more nines (99.999...%), which is greatly aided by checking multiple implementations. As things stand, these questions can always give up a few more nines while retreating back one step to a bug in the C++/rust compiler, a bug in the linux kernel, a bug in bash that reports the error code as 0 instead of 1, etc.

since lean use c++ internally for the kernel, it's worth mentioning that boost cpp also has an arbitrary precision number library called multiprecision.
It supports multiple backends and also a native cpp one. not sure this would add any confidence or better performance.

Chris Bailey said:

I've never directly worked on bignum code so I don't know how difficult or time consuming it would actually be, but having built-in bignums instead of using an external dependency would be neat.

It should be easy if one only implementing basic algorithms and without speed optimization. Maybe a pure Lean implementation using Array USize is feasible.

Kevin Buzzard said:

"how do you know Lean has got no bugs"

I don't think we can ever know for certain, in the absolute sense. We can only build an ever-growing confidence based on evidence:

  • Growing user base
  • Growing project variety to stress the system in different ways
  • Growing test suite to guarantee no regressions
  • Multiple independent kernel implementations

The Lean 4 source itself sits on top of an immense stack, if we take decades-old C++ compiler work into account.

Note that this same question applies to software that controls planes, hospital equipment, cars etc. The answer to critical software is not 100.00% satisfactory

Sure sure sure, the question is not "how do you know Lean has got no bugs" (which we can and have talked about at length elsewhere), the question is "how do you know AI is not abusing an overflow error in GMP"

Kevin Buzzard said:

Sure sure sure, the question is not "how do you know Lean has got no bugs" (which we can and have talked about at length elsewhere), the question is "how do you know AI is not abusing an overflow error in GMP"

Ask it to generate an audit trail? Or provide some information that can be separately audited? This would be in addition to whatever comparator uses: logs of activity that substantiate that the AI did what it said it did, or that the steps of the proof are each resolvable by a different implementation. (i.e. AI Z could use GMP but auditor Y (AI or not) could use some other bigint implementation to verify the computation.) Basically, you have to "look over its shoulder" at some point to answer such questions.

Henrik Böving said:

The question was this. Say a proof is AI-generated and the AI does the following malicious thing: finds a bug in GMP with e.g. some huge integers causing an overflow problem, proves false using it, and then deduces the Riemann hypothesis. At what, if any, point during the comparator and/or check-with-alternative-kernel procedure does this approach become unstuck?

If you want to prevent this type of scenario you have to use comparator with enable_nanoda set to true (and an installed nanoda of course). Nanoda uses num-bigint which is a pure Rust implementation of bignum arithmetic. While the code might be inspired by GMP (I don't know if it is) this is a fully separate implementation in another (notably memory safe) programming language so it should be unlikely that they allow for the exact same bugs.

As explained above there is no need to do that, we can deterministically ensure that it is not using a GMP bug this way

Is the GMP bug concern literal or does it represent a class of concern? Because using nanoda, with a different bignum implementation, just shifts the question (although it reduces the memory unsafety attack surface). Either way, the "solution" falls within the "multiple kernel implementations" category I mentioned above.

Feature proposal: the Lean 4 extension could be capable of managing side kernels. I mean an actual "Manage side kernels" button, which would allow users to add, remove or pause them. A side kernel would be a process that can stand as a server and follow a certain API contract. Side kernels would be independently configurable to raise warnings or errors. Under the hood, I think lean would be the one actually managing the communication, which would allow multiple kernels to be triggered directly via CLI without requiring interactions with the Lean 4 extension.

If you're at the point in your development where you're worried about this level of assurance (or this level of AI shenanigans), then Comparator is probably the tool you need to be using. Comparator does allow the management of side kernels. (Well, it assumes the side kernel is named nanoda_lib — but it absolutely makes sense to incorporate other side kernels when there's demand and other independent implementations that use the same interface as nanoda.)
For completeness, rpylean uses the rpython bigint implementation, so it's a third independent kernel with third different bigint implementation on the GMP-specific angle.
And depending on how exactly rpylean matches nanoda's specifcation format, you might already be able to run comparator with rpylean by just setting COMPARATOR_NANODA=rpylean

What I'm pointing at is something more integrated than a standalone implementation. That is, a "plug your kernel" API that comes out of the box, in official toolchain releases.

The reason is straightforward: there's this promise that users can use custom kernels to double/triple check proofs, but the integration requires ad-hoc tooling.
10 messages were moved here from #lean4 > comparator and GMP by Michael Rothgang.

The answer to the original question is "Comparator supports nanoda checking which does not depend on GMP" but FWIW, some time ago out of personal curiosity I implemented a version of comparator purely in Rust: https://github.com/hanwenzhu/nanocomparator. It is built on nanoda, does not depend on Lean (assuming the challenge/solution are already exported), and simply translates logic from the official Comparator. I am not sure if it is bug-free, but it demonstrates in principle that, like the kernel, Comparator's logic is a type theory property that can have independent implementations including this one that does not depend on GMP or C++ (hence less likely to have overflow/pointer problems).
